claims.text: An unspecified Mg-transition-metal alloy can be formulated with a density below 6 g/cm³.
Sintering the Mg-transition-metal alloy at 900 °C will produce a dense, single-phase-like microstructure with superior oxidation resistance.
High-strain-rate processing and elevated peak temperature can drive dynamic recrystallization and a BCC/B2-to-FCC transformation.
The cited strain-induced BCC/B2-to-FCC transformation will also occur in the proposed Mg-transition-metal alloy at 900 °C.
A short, high-strain-rate treatment at 900 °C will induce dynamic recrystallization while minimizing Mg volatility.
An FCC or FCC-L12 phase enriched in noble elements can act as a barrier protecting an underlying BCC-B2 phase.
The transient FCC fraction in the proposed Mg alloy will form a continuous, low-diffusivity surface layer that suppresses oxidation.
The transient FCC phase will stabilize the Mg alloy against elemental segregation.
At 1000 °C, the heterogeneous NV1 alloy has insufficient kinetics to form a dense continuous CrTaO4-based oxide layer, resulting in porous oxide, internal nitridation, and exponential mass gain.
The NV1 result establishes that temperatures above 1000 °C are kinetically insufficient for barrier continuity in the proposed Mg alloy.
Mn can diffuse outward during high-temperature exposure of CrMnFeCoNi, leaving a Mn-depleted subsurface region.
Severe Mn depletion and volatility generally occur above 1100 °C in the proposed Mg-transition-metal alloy.
The 900 °C process will yield greater than 95% relative density.
The 900 °C process will yield a grain size below 1 µm.
The 900 °C process will create a continuous protective oxide layer and reduce oxidation weight gain by more than 50% relative to processing at 800 °C or 1000 °C.
The final microstructure will be FCC-dominant and free of detrimental Laves phases and severe elemental segregation.
Standard sintering at 800 °C causes incomplete densification and poor barrier formation because diffusion kinetics are sluggish.
Standard sintering at 1000 °C causes heterogeneous oxidation and porous oxide layers in the proposed Mg alloy.
Below 850 °C, the proposed alloy will retain more than 5% porosity because of insufficient diffusion kinetics.
Above 1050 °C, or after an excessive dwell, Mg volatility and severe elemental depletion will occur.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the process must avoid an '800 °C volatility threshold,' whereas the baseline and boundary attribute the low-temperature failure to sluggish densification below 850 °C and place volatility above 1050 °C.

The hypothesis labels temperatures above 1000 °C as kinetically insufficient for barrier continuity, but the cited NV1 mechanism states that 1000 °C is insufficient while 1100 °C provides enough kinetics to form a denser layer.

The mechanism says 900 °C is high enough to ensure barrier-formation kinetics while describing failure at the higher temperature of 1000 °C; no internally established process distinction is quantified to resolve this temperature inversion.
The baseline identifies potential Mg volatility at 1000 °C, while the boundary places volatility and severe depletion only above 1050 °C.
